variants.name: record event with Spring ApplicationEventPublisher
variants.implementation_notes: A record (Java 16+) is the event contract: final components, generated accessors, equals/hashCode, no setters - the immutable event object the pattern calls for, with no need for an ApplicationEvent subclass since Spring 4.2 accepts any POJO in publishEvent(Object). @EventListener methods are dispatched by the listener's parameter type, so the publisher/subscriber wiring and the type-based routing live in the framework; cross-process delivery uses JMS or Kafka with a type header and a JsonSerializer/JsonDeserializer pair. The classic structure - an EventObject subclass with an EventListener registry - is still what happens underneath and remains the direct choice for Swing-style object-local notifications or when a framework demands it.
variants.idiom_name: record event + ApplicationEventPublisher/@EventListener (or a broker client)
pitfalls: Spring listeners run synchronously in the publisher's thread by default; without @Async or @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) a listener exception can fail or roll back the producing transaction.
Records are shallowly immutable: a mutable collection component lets a listener modify a published fact.
Serialising records with Jackson needs the parameter-names module (or explicit @JsonProperty) or the payload silently loses fields.
Routing on the concrete type means a listener registered for a supertype receives all subtypes; keep event hierarchies flat unless that is intended.

variants.name: java.util.EventObject subclass with an EventListener registry
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-records realizations on Java 8/11 - and still the shape exposed by AWT/Swing, JMS and many framework APIs - are a final class extending java.util.EventObject carrying the payload, an EventListener marker subinterface per event family, and a listener list (EventListenerList or a copy-on-write list) inside the publisher. The type hierarchy itself is the contract: the listener method signature selects the event type, and the publisher iterates its listener list. Choose it when integrating with an existing EventObject/EventListener API or when the codebase predates records; for new code the record plus a framework dispatcher is less ceremony with the same semantics.
pitfalls: The listener list must be thread-safe and iterated over a snapshot; notifying while listeners add or remove themselves corrupts the traversal.
Holding listener references prevents garbage collection of subscribers (listener leak): always offer removal and tie it to the subscriber's lifecycle.
Subclasses must stay final-ish and payload fields private final; EventObject only stores the source, so mutability creeps in through the subclass.
